children.translated_text: ... a handsome youth, as it were. Just as he delights, enters into the ecstasy of pleasure, and attains fame, the reputation of being fortunate — so too should the one of cultivated intellect be understood. ||

Through this path, the method of poetic treatise, properly shown, revealed — as the cause — fault being the portion to be rejected, and merit the one to be adopted — regarding these two as stated, related to practice, one whose intellect is cultivated, discriminating, capable of rejection and adoption — such a man, a knower of poetic faults and merits. Precisely for this reason, approached by submissive, obedient speeches in the form of poetry, faultless — one for whom the approach, the coming to him of its own accord, has been accomplished by speeches — thus approached, he delights, experiences unsurpassed pleasure. And fame —
let there be no jealousy toward the accumulated merit of this splendor of yours.
To declare a condition of praiseworthy form,
pleasing to the ear, praiseworthy poetic treatise of <s>Daṇḍin</s>. ||
Like a thing made of gold, this brilliant, resplendent,
even a trace of merit is today to be esteemed as weighty.
By those who observe an age filled with slender merits,
even a drop of [fresh] water is seen as delectable.
In a world bereft of clouds, where the flow is of brackish water,
possessing exceedingly abundant merit is not wondered at by us.
The virtuous accept even a trace of merit; therefore, their
somehow extend the state of being meritless — this is truly wondrous. ||
The wicked, however, despising even a great heap of merit,
a composition that is superior in merit is attended to by the wise.
Whether a poet of old or of today, clearly,
if sweet, is enjoyed without apprehension. ||
The fruit of a tree, whether ancient or new,
when touched by the matured word-compositions of poets.
Even an ordinary, common subject-matter becomes easy
even the most trivial thing attains the status of pure gold. ||
When composed by a connoisseur with flawless combinations of aesthetic savor,
the eye not empty but touched by droplets of tears born of joy,
The ear filled with nectar, the heart exalted with bliss,

children.text: दिदमिति किल काव्यं पठ्यते श्रूयते च ॥
children.translated_text: 'This indeed is poetry!' — thus it is recited and heard. ||
the body having attained horripilation — having savored this,
become worthy vessels for the hearing of fine speech.
Those whose intellects are canopies of special knowledge
spreads glory; but when displayed among beasts, it brings shame. ||
The aesthetic savor of poetry, when displayed among the wise,
whose pride has been calmed, who know distinctions —
Among those who delight in clear treatises, who love fine speech,
like clever women who have mastered the arts. ||
eloquent words attain a great festival,

children.text: दोषेष्वेव निवेशयन्ति हृदयं सर्वं खलास्ते कथं
कल्पन्ते गुणवैरिणो गुणवतां ज्ञात्वा गुणानां रसम् ।
children.translated_text: can these enemies of merit, having known the savor of merits, serve the meritorious?
The wicked fix their hearts only on faults — how then

children.text: दोषा[नेव हि] तत्र केवलममी पश्यन्ति [नित्यं सतां]

children.translated_text: abandoning the mighty heap of good qualities — ah, wondrous is the way of the wicked! ||
They see only faults there, always [among the virtuous],

children.text: लिप्सन्ते किल दुर्जनाः समतया संभावनां तादृशीम् ।
children.translated_text: the wicked indeed seek comparable esteem, as if by equality.
Through the audacity of false blame against the great, fallen from such distinction,

children.text: नायं हेतुरवाप्तये गुणभुवः कीर्तेः सतां संसदि
व्यामोहादपि वा गुणेषु पतनं तेषां यदेतद्बहु ॥
children.translated_text: or perhaps this great falling upon merits of theirs is out of sheer delusion. ||
This is not the means to attain fame born of merit in the assembly of the virtuous;
something else should be employed; this is worn out; this is novel; this should be examined thus' —
'This is the statement, and this is the substance; this is not appropriate here;
achieves success [in the eyes of critics]. ||
somehow, every literary composition
a drop of tears with horripilation, the calming [of the heart] —
This accumulated fruit of that labor —
this too, some bring to the state of jealousy
indeed. ||
the exaltation in the pleasure-chambers of the learned —
proceed to censure others.
Then, let the clever-minded one who would create something superior, something of such quality,
when what he proclaims is indeed an earache! ||
The erudition of the learned is false, O Creator,

children.text: न च विहतिः प्रकृतिस्तु तस्य सैषा ।
children.translated_text: are not impaired; that is simply their nature.
By the censure of the wicked, the merits
the wicked do not hate what is devoid of merit. ||
From this, this statement becomes evident:
like the rays of the moon,
The very merits that cool the minds of the wise,
or rather, where is there anything dear to the wicked? ||
if those very same burn the fire of the wicked —
by the radiant, brilliant merits of the meritorious, what destruction of him is there?
Is this a seat of suffering, entering the wicked? —

children.text: प्रीतिं परां सुजनवत् किमयं न भुङ्क्ते

children.translated_text: For the sake of delight alone is all human endeavor. ||
Does he not enjoy supreme delight, like a good person? —
one who causes suffering to others approaches the virtuous;
'They uplift others' — thus, with exceedingly cool [virtues],
the gulf between the good and the bad is exceedingly vast. ||
by his own lofty merits, this unstated [truth reveals itself] —
should not be disregarded by the learned.
The speech of the virtuous, whose merits are intact, regarding both self and other,
destroys both self and other, be accepted? ||
How can the verbal poison of the wicked, which in every way
is nowhere established as authoritative.
What has been done, whether blamed or praised,
shame on such mockery that lacks self-knowledge! ||
And if one desires to speak in such a manner —
and with rivalry toward equals,
Burning with blazing jealousy toward those of superior merit,
by whom should this wicked person be loved? ||
and with causeless contempt toward inferiors —
he does not himself tread the path of merit.
If he is instructed, the form burns;
no medicine for him exists other than avoidance. ||
How is this wicked one to be treated? —
and there instructs others too.
The evil-minded plunges into fault in preference to merit,
he does not let go, out of fear of the defeat of his position. ||
Even having somehow learned from another,
that one who treads the path of blame — from afar,
Thus, corrupted by the false pride of pseudo-scholars,
as if bitten by time [i.e., as one avoids the incurable]. ||
these virtuous ones, knowers of right conduct, avoid him
and rains it upon those of lesser attainment.
The devoted one, from one of superior merit, drinks the nectar of merit
the gracious person shares discourse. ||
Together with equals, pursuing the path of its increase,
how much more then by deeds that are made of merit!
The good person brings happiness even by name alone —
like a serpent, terrifies in both ways. ||
But this wicked one, wrathful without cause,
clear as the autumn moon, wise —
Those who are brilliant with wondrous genius, accomplished,
The wicked one alone is not pleased with them. ||
whose mind do they not captivate?
the wicked one too does not cease from behavior lacking merit.
The good person does not cease from virtuous conduct;
has come about somehow through circumstance. ||
The difference between the two that has remained
to the good person, the repository of merits — salutation!
In every way, to the virtuous, whose nature purifies the world,
cast aside wickedness! ||
May the intellect of the wicked, devoted to good qualities,
whose unbridled power is death to his enemies, the abode of meritorious qualities,
Of him who is the ornamental mark of the <s>Rāṣṭrakūṭa</s> dynasty, exalted above all, whose praise has not ceased in song,
of the glorious king <s>Tuṅga</s> — the wise have such patronage as this. ||
whose lotus feet are graced by <s>Lakṣmī</s>, the victorious one, the crest-jewel of feudatory lords —
The renown of the learned, through the support of the lofty mountain <s>Tuṅga</s>,
flows forth like great rivers whose course serves the world's purpose. ||
The one known as <s>Yaśakīrti</s>, the glorious one, from the (...) lineage,
was the spiritual friend (<s>kalyāṇamitra</s>) here — a monk (<s>bhikṣu</s>), the ornament of <s>Sindhu</s>. ||
Another says —
The speech of debaters today is heavy with downpour, unfortunate;
the learned discourse of <s>Ratnaśrījñāna</s> is arranged in the opposite manner [i.e., clear and delightful]. ||
Thus ends the third chapter, on the difficult [path], in the commentary on <s>Daṇḍin's</s> Poetic Treatise, named <s>Ratnaśrī</s>. ||

body.translated_text: || Thus is completed this commentary, the <s>Ratnaśrī</s>. ||
|| This is the work of the teacher <s>Ratnaśrījñāna</s>, born in <s>Siṃhala</s> (Sri Lanka). ||
|| This commentary was composed in the twenty-third regnal year of the king <s>Rājyapāla</s>. ||
